whatWasRun: Three full rollback -> reapply cycles against real hosted staging, using all 8 accepted rollback scripts in reverse candidate order and all 8 accepted forward candidates in forward order. Every file was sha256-verified against the accepted set before use.

digests.digestScope: schemas, relations, columns, functions (including body md5), policies, triggers, table grants and column grants across public, private, storage AND limiter. Broader than migrations-next/phase03a/catalog.sql, which does not cover the limiter schema.

determinism.fullJsonByteComparison: The complete 349,583-byte structural JSON from cycle 1 and cycle 2 are byte-identical.
determinism.conclusion: Rollback and reapply are each deterministic and the pair converges to a fixed point. Restoration is repeatable, not lucky.

restorationDoesNotBreakShippedClients.meaning: A production rollback would restore the pre-03A posture WITHOUT breaking Build 33 clients. That is the property that makes the rollback usable in an incident.

behaviouralEquivalenceAfterReapply.hosted_FDA028_acceptance_plan38: 0 failures, reproduced on 4 runs after reapply
behaviouralEquivalenceAfterReapply.vaultSecretSurvived: fda028_limiter_epoch_key still present after the round trip (metadata only — the value was never selected, printed or logged). The limiter re-derives its epoch key from Vault after the schema is recreated, which is why the FDA-028 suite passes on a freshly reapplied schema.
behaviouralEquivalenceAfterReapply.conclusion: The reapplied catalog is behaviourally equivalent on every assertion the accepted artifact set defines.

divergenceFinding.severity: MUST-FIX BEFORE ANY PRODUCTION ROLLBACK IS RELIED UPON
divergenceFinding.statement: DIGEST_AFTER_REAPPLY (c70e119a) does not equal DIGEST_POST_APPLY (09c42928). A rollback followed by a reapply lands on a structurally different catalog than a clean first apply, even though both pass all 286 hosted assertions.
divergenceFinding.whyItHappens_bestSupportedExplanation: The accepted rollbacks are FORWARD-RESTORATION scripts, not exact inverse DDL. The posture they reconstruct is therefore not guaranteed byte-identical to the true pre-03A posture, and reapplying the forward candidates on top of an approximated baseline lands on a stable but different state. The apply MECHANISM is not the cause: DDL semantics do not depend on whether a statement arrived via the Management API or the CLI.
divergenceFinding.whyItCouldNotBeLocalisedExactly: I hashed the original post-apply state but did NOT retain its full structural JSON, so the original cannot be diffed field-by-field. This is my error in checkpoint discipline and is recorded as such rather than hidden.

whatWasLocalised.method: Diffed the rolled-back posture (535,171 bytes) against the reapplied posture (349,583 bytes) to characterise what Phase 03A actually does.
whatWasLocalised.phase03aAdds: the limiter schema, 5 relations, 27 columns, 27 functions, 1 trigger, and the RESTRICTIVE policy public.flags :: 'flags authenticated insert open' (FDA-009)
whatWasLocalised.phase03aRemoves: public.flags :: flags_user_scoped (the broad ALL policy) and public.users :: 'users readable by authenticated' (FDA-026)
whatWasLocalised.phase03aRewrites: 3 admin-delete policies (same names, changed definitions) on public.flags, public.flag_comments and storage.objects
whatWasLocalised.assessment: Every observed difference in this direction is an intended Phase 03A effect. Nothing anomalous was found in the rolled-back-vs-reapplied comparison itself.

requiredBeforeProduction: Capture and RETAIN the full structural JSON (not just its hash) immediately before and immediately after any production apply.
Rehearse the production rollback with both JSONs retained, and identify the exact field-level delta before relying on the rollback in an incident.

Decide explicitly whether the accepted rollbacks should be tightened into exact inverses, or whether a stable-but-different restored state is acceptable given 286/286 behavioural equivalence. This is an owner decision, not mine to assume.

furtherLocalisationAttempted.attempt: Static scan pairing each rollback script's GRANT statements against its forward candidate's REVOKE statements, looking for a grant the rollback restores that the forward candidate never takes back — which would persist into the reapplied state and explain the divergence.
furtherLocalisationAttempted.result: INCONCLUSIVE — not reported as a finding.
furtherLocalisationAttempted.why: The matcher compares statement text, so it cannot tell that one broad REVOKE covers many narrow GRANTs. It flagged entries in 7 candidates, but the only wildcard REVOKEs in the whole forward set are the three limiter-scoped ones in 20260909120000, so the flags could be neither confirmed nor dismissed from text alone.
furtherLocalisationAttempted.whatIsAuthoritativeInstead: The catalog itself. Reapply reduces table grants 543 -> 266 and column grants 2309 -> 1386, and the hosted privileges pgTAP suite (plan 79) plus the role/authorization matrix (plan 31) assert the intended privilege posture directly. Both pass with 0 failures after the round trip, so the reapplied privilege posture is asserted-correct even though the structural digest differs from the first apply.
furtherLocalisationAttempted.honestStatus: The divergence is real, stable and reproducible, and it is NOT in the privilege posture that the accepted suites assert. Beyond that it is unlocalised, and localising it requires the retained first-apply structural JSON that I failed to keep.

ledgerNote_ELEVATED.raisedBy: independent staging acceptor (SHOULD-FIX); the author under-weighted it
ledgerNote_ELEVATED.fact: The rollback scripts never unwind supabase_migrations.schema_migrations. The six phase03a_* ledger rows survived all three rollback cycles.
ledgerNote_ELEVATED.authorsOriginalFraming: 'inherent to any rollback, and resolved once reapply completes' — true for THIS rehearsal, which always reapplied.
ledgerNote_ELEVATED.whyThatWasTooKind: In a real incident the database stays rolled back. It would then still claim those migrations are applied, so a later `db push` or `migration up` would skip re-applying them. Combined with the separate finding that the recorded versions are wall-clock rather than canonical, and that two candidates have no ledger row at all, the migration ledger cannot be trusted as a record of what is applied.
